rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Pharaoh's insult amounts to denying Moses' allegation that any lord exists other than Pharaoh himself.
rows.anchor: “There is nothing to his allegation that there is a Lord other than me” (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' reply continues describing God's creation and lordship, contrasting Pharaoh's bounded dominion with God's all-encompassing sovereignty.
rows.anchor: differentiate Pharaoh’s limited and finite dominion from the all-encompassing sovereignty of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' threefold answer does not reveal God's unknowable ultimate nature; it points to means by which knowledge of God may be attained.
rows.anchor: impossible since God’s ultimate nature is not knowable—but rather to suggest the means by which one can attain that knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's question also appears when he addresses his father and people in 6:74 and asks about the images his people follow in 21:52.
rows.anchor: This question is also stated in 6:74, where Abraham addresses his father and his people

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAjībah presents the Abrahamic ḥanīf as an ideal of pure primordial monotheism untouched by sectarian tribalism.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAjībah notes that the Abrahamic ḥanīf (see 2:135c; 3:95; 4:125; 6:161), the ideal

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this story Abraham renounces every lord but God.
rows.anchor: where Abraham renounces all lords but God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham calls enemies the things that occupy the heart in place of God and people who follow egotistical passions.
rows.anchor: names as enemies those things that occupy the heart in place of God and those people who follow their egotistical passions

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The idolaters concede that their idols have no power to harm or benefit them.
rows.anchor: The idolaters admit that the idols do not have the power to harm or benefit (IK)

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī treats reliance on inherited authority as an argument against taqlīd and for belief grounded in sound reasoning and proof.
rows.anchor: This is, for al-Rāzī, a clear argument against belief based on conformity with authority

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Abraham's answer shows that an error remains wrong whether recent or entrenched, regardless of the authority invoked for it.
rows.anchor: Abraham’s reply shows that error, whether recent or entrenched, is error regardless of the authority to which one defers in upholding it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source links this rejection of ancestral imitation to 5:104 and similar injunctions in 7:28, 10:78, 28:36, 31:21, and 43:24.
rows.anchor: For the notion of idolaters blindly following the ways of their forefathers, see commentary on 5:104

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: One interpretation takes they to mean the idol worshippers rather than the idols themselves.
rows.anchor: Another interpretation is that the they refers to those who worship the idols and not the idols themselves (R)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: On this reading, the exception means those who worship the Lord of the worlds.
rows.anchor: In this interpretation, the subsequent phrase would be understood to mean, “except those who worship the Lord of the worlds” (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's statement may imply that his people worshipped the Lord of the worlds alongside idols, as the Quraysh did.
rows.anchor: Abraham’s statement seems to suggest that the Lord of the worlds was among those beings or things worshipped by his people along with their idols

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham clarifies that his enmity is directed at idols and false objects of worship, not at the Lord of the worlds.
rows.anchor: Abraham wanted to make clear that he was only expressing enmity toward the idols and false objects of worship and not the Lord of the worlds

rows.speaker: Su
rows.claim: Spiritually, one must make worldly things an enemy before truly loving God.
rows.anchor: one has to make the things of the world one’s enemy before one can truly love God (Su)

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says idol worship can make idols seem to their worshippers like destructive, corruptive living beings, thus enemies to Abraham.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī reasons that enemies unto me can also mean that, because of the worship afforded to the idols by his people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only a being capable of the listed acts is worthy of worship.
rows.anchor: Only a being capable of the acts listed in these verses is worthy and deserving of worship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Symbolically, God nourishes the soul, heals its ailments, and enlivens the spirit by bringing death to the passionate ego.
rows.anchor: Interpreted symbolically, these verses can mean that God feeds and nourishes the soul, heals the ailments of the soul, and enlivens the spirit

rows.speaker: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq
rows.claim: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq is reported to say that when sin makes him ill, God heals him with repentance.
rows.anchor: A saying attributed toJaʿfar al-Ṣādiq states, “When I am ill through sin, He heals me with repentance”

rows.speaker: Su
rows.claim: Some say the food signifies faith, while the drink signifies trust in God and contentment.
rows.anchor: Others say that the food is faith, and the drink is trust in God and contentment (Su)

rows.speaker: Al-Thaʿlabī
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī describes spiritual death and life as justice and grace, disobedience and obedience, separation and meeting God, and ignorance and knowledge.
rows.anchor: Al-Thaʿlabī summarizes the spiritual dimensions of these verses by saying that God brings death through justice and life through grace

rows.speaker: Su
rows.claim: Others say people die outwardly yet live inwardly, die through forgetting God, and live through remembering Him.
rows.anchor: one is caused to die outwardly, but is given life inwardly, dies through forgetfulness of God, and lives through remembrance of Him (Su)

rows.speaker: Junayd
rows.claim: Junayd compares resurrection to nakedness, hunger, and thirst, except for those clothed in reverence and given gnosis and love.
rows.anchor: Some quote Junayd, who says that when human beings are resurrected on the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nearly all Muslim theologians maintain that prophets are sinless or promised forgiveness for their sins.
rows.anchor: Practically all Muslim theologians espouse the principle that the prophets are without sin or are promised forgiveness for their sins

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some struggle with Abraham's request for forgiveness because hope expresses aspiration rather than certainty of fulfillment.
rows.anchor: some have difficulty with the idea that Abraham might hope for forgiveness, which expresses an aspiration rather than certitude

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others wrestle with Abraham's apparent attribution of sin to himself.
rows.anchor: while others wrestle with Abraham’s apparent attribution of sin to himself

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: For Abraham, hope can mean certainty, whereas for believers it expresses yearning.
rows.anchor: For some it means that, in the case of Abraham, “hope” is a kind of certainty, but for believers it is a yearning (Q)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Others say Abraham's words serve as an example and teach Muslims how to make proper supplications.
rows.anchor: others say that Abraham’s words are meant to be an example and provide Muslims with a way to make proper supplications (R)

rows.speaker: Mujāhid
rows.claim: Mujāhid says Abraham's hoped-for sin may refer to the idol story in 21:63 and to the episodes involving the stars in 6:76 and 37:89, which outwardly seem to show a failure to affirm God alone.
rows.anchor: Mujāhid says that it could refer to 21:63, where Abraham “lies” and tells the people the largest idol destroyed all the others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and children, sources of worldly status, security, and comfort, are useless in the Hereafter; this is a recurring Quranic theme.
rows.anchor: The uselessness in the Hereafter of wealth and children, which exalt human beings and are a source of security, status, and comfort in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sound heart is also associated with Abraham.
rows.anchor: A sound heart is also associated with Abraham

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q says a sound heart knows that God is real, the Hereafter will come, and God will resurrect the dead in their graves.
rows.anchor: it refers to knowing that God is real, that the Hereafter will come, and that God will resurrect what is in the graves (Q)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ says a sound heart is free of doubts and sincere.
rows.anchor: a heart without doubts and one that is sincere (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: IK says a sound heart is free of polytheism.
rows.anchor: sincere (Ṭ) and free of polytheism (IK)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R says a sound heart is free of ignorance, vices, and attachments to worldly life.
rows.anchor: ignorance, vices, and attachments to the life of this world (R)

rows.speaker: Th
rows.claim: Th describes it as a spiritually healthy heart rather than a sick one.
rows.anchor: the heart that is spiritually healthy as opposed to one that is sick (Th)

rows.speaker: Su
rows.claim: Su describes the sound heart as empty of all but its Lord and happy only with Him.
rows.anchor: a heart that is empty of all but its Lord and only happy with Him (Su)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q classifies al-Naml as a Makkan sūrah.
rows.anchor: A Makkan sūrah (Q), al-Naml

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Naml takes its name from the valley of ants traversed by Solomon's army.
rows.anchor: takes its name from the valley of the ants through which Solomon’s army passes, mentioned in v. 18

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening verses invoke common Quranic themes about the Final Judgment.
rows.anchor: opens with several verses articulating common themes in the Quran regarding Final Judgment in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account then recounts Moses encountering fire on the mountain, where God charged him to go to Pharaoh and free the Israelites.
rows.anchor: turns to Moses’ encounter with the fire on the mountain, from which God spoke charging him with his mission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of Solomon's miraculous host and encounter with the Queen of Sheba ends with her embracing faith in the One God.
rows.anchor: Solomon with his miraculous host of men, jinn, and birds and his encounter with the Queen of Sheba, who eventually comes before Solomon

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah recounts the Arabian prophet Ṣāliḥ and the Thamūd, including their plot to murder him.
rows.anchor: The story of the Arabian prophet Ṣāliḥ and his people, the Thamūd, is recounted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot's story briefly describes the destruction of his people for their iniquities.
rows.anchor: Lot’s story, including the destruction of his people for their iniquities, is told briefly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sequence invites reflection on God and creation, punctuated by the refrain asking whether there is a god alongside God.
rows.anchor: the refrain Is there a god alongside God? punctuates the passage several times

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers challenge bodily resurrection and the end of the world; the passage reminds readers God alone knows the hidden in heaven, earth, and human hearts.
rows.anchor: The disbelievers challenge the Prophet regarding the reality of bodily resurrection and the coming of the end of the world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah says God will judge between those who differ on religious matters.
rows.anchor: Verses describing how God will judge between those who differ on religious matters

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing section treats eschatological signs and events, including the beast, gathering religious communities, terror, the mountains' destruction, and consequences for good and evil.
rows.anchor: eschatological realities, such as the “beast” that will rise as one of the portents of the end of the world
